articles.title: Why We Perform Wudu
articles.summary: The purification before prayer, and what it represents.
articles.body: Wudu is the ritual washing Muslims perform before prayer, described in the Qur'an (5:6) and practiced in essentially the same form since the earliest generation of Muslims. On one level, it is simple hygiene — washing the hands, face, arms, and feet. But it is also treated as a spiritual preparation: a way of consciously setting aside the concerns of the moment and approaching prayer in a state of cleanliness and readiness. Many scholars have noted that the parts of the body washed are also the parts most exposed to daily interaction with the world — the hands that act, the face that meets others, the feet that carry us. Performing wudu attentively, rather than rushing through it, is often recommended as a way to begin shifting one's focus toward prayer before it even begins.

articles.title: Getting Started with the Five Daily Prayers
articles.summary: A gentle starting point for building the habit of Salah.
articles.body: For someone new to praying five times a day, the idea can feel overwhelming at first. It helps to remember that the prayers are spread naturally across the day — before sunrise, midday, afternoon, sunset, and night — so they become checkpoints in your day rather than one large task. Start by learning the movements and words of a single prayer well, using a guide or a step-by-step resource, and build from there. It is normal to need to check notes or repeat steps in the beginning. Many people find it easier to build the habit prayer by prayer, starting with whichever one fits most naturally into their current routine, rather than trying to change everything at once. Consistency matters more than perfection, especially at the start.

articles.title: Understanding the Five Pillars
articles.summary: The core framework that Islamic practice is built around.
articles.body: The Five Pillars are the foundational acts of worship in Islam: the declaration of faith (Shahada), the five daily prayers (Salah), obligatory charity (Zakat), fasting during Ramadan (Sawm), and pilgrimage to Makkah (Hajj) for those who are able. They are often introduced together because they form a structure that touches belief, daily practice, community responsibility, self-discipline, and once-in-a-lifetime devotion. Rather than five separate obligations, they work together: prayer keeps faith present day to day, charity connects personal wealth to the wellbeing of others, fasting builds self-restraint, and pilgrimage draws the global Muslim community together in one place. Learning them as a set, rather than in isolation, helps make sense of why each one is there.

articles.title: The Virtue of Friday
articles.summary: Why Jumu'ah holds a special place in the week.
articles.body: Friday holds a distinct status in Islam, centered on the communal Jumu'ah prayer that replaces the midday prayer for those attending it. Beyond the obligation itself, many Muslims treat Friday as an occasion for extra reflection — reciting Surah Al-Kahf, increasing in supplication, and taking a moment to slow down in the middle of the week. The communal nature of the Jumu'ah prayer is part of its significance: it is a weekly gathering that reconnects individuals to their local community, in a way the five daily prayers, often performed individually, do not always provide. Treating Friday as a slightly different day — rather than an ordinary one — is a small, achievable way to build more rhythm into a week.

articles.title: The Importance of Sincerity in Worship
articles.summary: Why the intention behind an act often matters as much as the act itself.
articles.body: Ikhlas, sincerity, is the idea that acts of worship are meant to be done for the sake of God alone, without seeking praise or recognition from others. It is easy to focus only on whether an act of worship was performed correctly — the right words, the right movements — while giving less thought to why it was performed. Islamic teaching consistently returns to intention as the starting point of any act: a well-known hadith opens with the statement that actions are judged by their intentions. Practically, this means it can be worth pausing, occasionally, to ask not just "did I do this?" but "why did I do this?" — a habit that tends to deepen the meaning of worship over time rather than leaving it as routine.
